claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially in a high-temperature BCC state.
Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed primarily by diffusion-mediated development of local compositional inhomogeneities.
Preferential Al segregation is the particularly important compositional inhomogeneity governing phase stability.
Local regions exceeding a critical Al concentration become thermodynamically unstable and nucleate and grow secondary phases.
Increasing annealing dwell time at a fixed temperature increases the extent of Al diffusion.
Rapid quenching preserves the high-temperature microstructure for subsequent characterization.
The relevant structural mediator is nanoscale Al segregation at grain boundaries or within sub-grain regions.
Longer high-temperature annealing allows Al to preferentially accumulate in localized regions.
Local Al enrichment beyond a critical threshold destabilizes homogeneous BCC and drives FCC or intermetallic nucleation.
At a given temperature, longer annealing times will produce a higher volume fraction of secondary phases.
Longer annealing times will produce more pronounced local Al concentration gradients.
Samples annealed for approximately five minutes will largely retain homogeneous BCC with minimal segregation.
The proposed Al-segregation mechanism dominates between 1100 and 1350 °C when diffusion is significant.
Extensive grain growth can become a competing effect at sufficiently long high-temperature exposures.
At significantly lower temperatures, mechanisms other than diffusion-mediated Al segregation may govern phase stability.
The critical Al concentration and quantitative diffusion coefficients and activation energies remain undetermined.
Failure to observe a statistically significant increase in both secondary-phase fraction and local Al enrichment with dwell time would falsify Al segregation as the primary driver.
